desc:
Given a string s of lowercase letters, return the lexicographically smallest subsequence of s that contains every distinct letter of s exactly once. A subsequence keeps the original relative order of the characters it keeps.

Example: s = "cbacdcbc" gives "acdb", and s = "bcabc" gives "abc".
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Every distinct letter has to appear once, so the answer has as many characters as there are distinct letters. The question is which occurrence of each letter to keep.

Build the answer from left to right. When a new letter c arrives and the last kept letter is larger than c, removing that larger letter would improve the result, but only if it still occurs later in the string.

Keep a stack for the answer, a set of letters already on the stack, and the last index of each letter. Skip letters already on the stack. Otherwise pop while the top is larger than c and appears again later, then push c.
editorial: Scan left to right with a stack that holds the answer so far. A letter that is already on the stack is skipped: the earlier copy sits at least as far left, which can only help. For a new letter c, look at the top of the stack. If the top is larger than c and the same letter occurs again later in s, then dropping it and placing it later gives a smaller string and loses nothing, so pop it and repeat. Finally push c.

The condition 'occurs again later' is answered in O(1) from a table of last occurrences, and membership from a boolean array of 26 entries. Each character is pushed and popped at most once, so the time is O(n) and the extra space is O(1) besides the stack (at most 26 characters). This is the same greedy as 'remove k digits', except that the amount we may delete is dictated by which letters still have a spare copy ahead.
